Utilities#

Helpers for names, sequences, tensor construction and numerical operations.

Strings and names#

tensorkrowch.utils.print_list(lst)[source]#
tensorkrowch.utils.tab_string(string, num_tabs=1)[source]#

Introduces ‘ ‘ a certain amount of times before each line.

Parameters

  • string (str) – Text to be displaced.

  • num_tabs (int) – Number of ‘ ‘ introduced.

Return type

str

tensorkrowch.utils.check_name_style(name, type='axis')[source]#

Axis’ names can only contain letters, numbers and underscores. Nodes’ names cannot contain blank spaces.

tensorkrowch.utils.erase_enum(name)[source]#

Given a name, returns the same name without any enumeration suffix with format _{digit}.

tensorkrowch.utils.enum_repeated_names(names_list)[source]#

Given a list of (axes or nodes) names, returns the same list but adding an enumeration for the names that appear more than once in the list.

Sequences and permutations#

tensorkrowch.utils.permute_list(lst, dims)[source]#

Permutes elements of list based on a permutation of indices. It is not required that lst and dims have the same length; in such case the returned list will only have as many elements as indices specified in dims, in the corresponding order.

Parameters

  • lst (list) – List to be permuted.

  • dims (list[int]) – List of dimensions (indices) in the new order.

tensorkrowch.utils.is_permutation(lst, permuted_lst)[source]#

Indicates if permuted_lst is a permutation of the elements of lst.

tensorkrowch.utils.inverse_permutation(dims)[source]#

Given a permutation of indices (to permute the elements of a list, tensor, etc.), returns the inverse permutation of indices needed to recover the original object (in the original order).

Parameters

dims (list[int]) – Permutation of indices. It can be complete if all numbers in range(len(dims)) appear (e.g. (2, 0, 1) -> (1, 2, 0)), or incomplete if after permutation some elements were removed (e.g. (3, 0, 2) -> (1, 2, 0), removed element in position 1).

tensorkrowch.utils.list2slice(lst)[source]#

Given a list (of indices) returns, if possible, an object slice containing the same indices.

tensorkrowch.utils.split_sequence_into_regions(lst)[source]#

Splits a sequence of integers into regions where each region contains consecutive integers.

Parameters

lst (list[int] or tuple[int]) – List of integers in ascending order.

Return type

list[list[int]]

Raises

  • TypeError – If the input is not a sequence of integers.

  • ValueError – If the input sequence is not ordered.

Example

>>> sequence = [1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 13]
>>> tk.utils.split_sequence_into_regions(sequence)
[[1, 2, 3], [5, 6, 7], [10, 11], [13]]

Combinatorics#

tensorkrowch.utils.fact(n)[source]#

Returns factorial of n.

tensorkrowch.utils.binomial_coeffs(n, k)[source]#

Tensor construction#

tensorkrowch.utils.stack_unequal_tensors(lst_tensors)[source]#

Stacks a list of tensors. These tensors need not have equal sizes in each dimension, but they must have the same rank.

The smallest tensors are extended with zeros to match the shape of the biggest ones.

Parameters

lst_tensors (list[torch.Tensor]) – List of tensors to be stacked

Return type

torch.Tensor

tensorkrowch.utils.random_unitary(n, device=None, dtype=None, generator=None)[source]#

Returns random unitary matrix from the Haar measure of size n x n.

Unitary matrix is created as described in this paper.

generator controls the Gaussian matrix without modifying the global random state and should belong to the requested device.

Tensor scaling and normalization#

These operations are shared by formats and decomposition algorithms. They retain PyTorch broadcasting, devices and autograd. A zero tensor remains zero under normalization with extracted log-scale 0; its mathematical log-norm is -inf.

tensorkrowch.utils.safe_divide(numerator, denominator, zero_value=0)[source]#

Divides tensors, substituting zero_value wherever the denominator is zero.

The denominator is made safe before division, including in branches that are later discarded. PyTorch broadcasting, device and dtype rules apply.

Parameters

  • numerator (torch.Tensor) – Tensors to divide elementwise, with broadcastable shapes.

  • denominator (torch.Tensor) – Tensors to divide elementwise, with broadcastable shapes.

  • zero_value (number or torch.Tensor) – Result at zero denominators. Defaults to 0; a tensor must be broadcastable with the quotient.

Returns

Quotient with the requested values at zero denominators.

Return type

torch.Tensor

Examples

>>> tk.utils.safe_divide(torch.tensor([2., 0.]), torch.tensor([4., 0.]))
tensor([0.5000, 0.0000])
tensorkrowch.utils.scale_tensor(tensor, dim=None, keepdim=False)[source]#

Extracts a maximum-magnitude scale before numerical tensor operations.

Zero reductions use scale 1, leaving their values unchanged. For complex tensors, the maximum absolute real or imaginary component is used so that forming a complex magnitude cannot overflow before scaling.

Parameters

  • tensor (torch.Tensor) – Real floating or complex tensor. The input is not modified.

  • dim (int or sequence of int, optional) – Axes over which to extract the scale. Defaults to all axes.

  • keepdim (bool) – Retains reduced axes of size 1 in the returned scale when True. The scaled tensor always retains its original shape.

Returns

Scaled tensor and its real, positive scale. Multiplying by the scale, with reduced axes restored when necessary, reconstructs the input.

Return type

tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]

Examples

>>> scaled, scale = tk.utils.scale_tensor(torch.tensor([3., -6.]))
>>> scaled
tensor([ 0.5000, -1.0000])
>>> scale
tensor(6.)
tensorkrowch.utils.stable_norm(tensor, dim=None, keepdim=False)[source]#

Computes an L2 norm after extracting the tensor’s largest component.

Scaling avoids overflow or underflow while squaring the input values. A norm outside the dtype’s representable range may still overflow; use log_tensor_norm() when the norm itself need not be materialized.

Parameters

  • tensor (torch.Tensor) – Real floating or complex tensor.

  • dim (int or sequence of int, optional) – Reduction axes. Defaults to all axes, giving the Frobenius norm.

  • keepdim (bool) – Retains reduced axes of size 1 when True.

Returns

Real norm, with zero returned for zero or empty reductions.

Return type

torch.Tensor

Examples

>>> tk.utils.stable_norm(torch.tensor([3., 4.]))
tensor(5.)
tensorkrowch.utils.log_tensor_norm(tensor, dim=None, keepdim=False)[source]#

Computes the natural logarithm of an L2 norm without materializing the norm.

Parameters

  • tensor (torch.Tensor) – Real floating or complex tensor.

  • dim (int or sequence of int, optional) – Reduction axes. Defaults to all axes, giving the log Frobenius norm.

  • keepdim (bool) – Retains reduced axes of size 1 when True.

Returns

Real log-norm. Zero or empty reductions have log-norm -inf.

Return type

torch.Tensor

Examples

>>> tk.utils.log_tensor_norm(torch.tensor([0., 0.]))
tensor(-inf)
tensorkrowch.utils.normalize_tensor(tensor, dim=None)[source]#

Normalizes a tensor and returns the logarithmic scale extracted from it.

Maximum-component scaling precedes the L2 normalization, so the original norm need not be representable. Zero reductions remain zero and contribute log-scale 0. Use log_tensor_norm() for their actual log-norm.

Parameters

  • tensor (torch.Tensor) – Real floating or complex tensor. The input is not modified.

  • dim (int or sequence of int, optional) – Axes to normalize jointly. Defaults to all axes.

Returns

Normalized tensor and real log-scale, with reduction axes removed. Autograd is retained through both outputs.

Return type

tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]

Examples

>>> normalized, log_scale = tk.utils.normalize_tensor(torch.tensor([3., 4.]))
>>> normalized
tensor([0.6000, 0.8000])
>>> log_scale.exp()
tensor(5.)
tensorkrowch.utils.ratio_from_log(log_numerator, log_denominator)[source]#

Computes a ratio of non-negative magnitudes from their natural logarithms.

Subtracts the logarithms before exponentiating, avoiding overflow from materializing the two magnitudes separately. Zero is represented by -inf; 0 / 0 is defined as 0 and a positive magnitude divided by zero gives inf.

Parameters

  • log_numerator (torch.Tensor) – Real logarithms with broadcastable shapes, on the same device.

  • log_denominator (torch.Tensor) – Real logarithms with broadcastable shapes, on the same device.

Returns

Ratio with the documented zero-denominator convention.

Return type

torch.Tensor

Examples

>>> tk.utils.ratio_from_log(torch.tensor([1000., -torch.inf]),
...                         torch.tensor([1000., -torch.inf]))
tensor([1., 0.])
tensorkrowch.utils.norm_from_log(log_norm, reference_norm=None)[source]#

Reconstructs a magnitude from its natural logarithm using an optional scale.

A positive reference expresses the magnitude relative to that scale before multiplying it back. A zero reference uses scale 1; it does not change the reconstructed magnitude. Values outside the dtype’s representable range can still overflow or underflow.

Parameters

  • log_norm (torch.Tensor) – Real logarithm of a non-negative magnitude. -inf represents zero.

  • reference_norm (torch.Tensor, optional) – Finite, non-negative reference with a broadcastable shape on the same device. Without a reference, returns log_norm.exp().

Returns

Reconstructed non-negative magnitude.

Return type

torch.Tensor

Examples

>>> tk.utils.norm_from_log(torch.tensor([0., -torch.inf]), torch.zeros(2))
tensor([1., 0.])

Singular-value decompositions#

tensorkrowch.utils.accurate_svd(tensor, recursion_threshold=0.0001, max_depth=16)[source]#

Computes an economy-size SVD with recursive refinement of small values.

Implements the Appendix of Stoudenmire and White’s Real-Space Parallel Density Matrix Renormalization Group. After the initial SVD, the small-value subspace is projected from the original matrix and decomposed recursively. A single SVD may resolve the largest singular values well while losing relative accuracy in much smaller ones. Refinement isolates that tail in a smaller matrix, recomputes its SVD and updates the associated singular vectors. This repeats only when the smaller matrix still has a separated tail, up to the recursion limit.

This can improve relative accuracy in the tail, but cannot recover values lost when forming the input or guarantee relative accuracy below its floating-point resolution. No singular values are truncated or inverted.

The backend is selected by get_svd_method(), including overrides from svd_method(), and is fixed throughout recursion. This function always attempts refinement, independently of get_svd_refinement().

Parameters

  • tensor (torch.Tensor) – Finite floating-point or complex matrix with shape (*, m, n). Leading batch dimensions and empty matrix dimensions are supported; each matrix may select a different refinement subspace. Dtype and dimensionality validation is delegated to the PyTorch backend.

  • recursion_threshold (float) – Relative threshold in (0, 1) for selecting the small-value tail at each level: refine values satisfying s[i] / s[0] < threshold. Default is 1e-4. Larger thresholds include more values in the refinement; this is neither a truncation tolerance nor an error bound.

  • max_depth (int) – Maximum number of additional SVD refinement levels after the initial SVD. Default is 16. Zero returns the unrefined economy-size SVD. Recursion stops earlier if no tail is selected, the subspace has only one singular value, or all singular values are zero.

Returns

(u, s, vh) with shapes (*, m, r), (*, r), (*, r, n) and r = min(m, n). Device and core dtype are preserved; singular values use the corresponding real dtype. Uses PyTorch exclusively.

Return type

tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]

Raises

  • TypeError – If tensor or refinement controls have invalid types.

  • ValueError – If a refinement control is outside its accepted interval.

  • RuntimeError – If the PyTorch backend rejects the tensor’s dtype or dimensions, or the decomposition does not converge.

Notes

Batch-specific refinement decisions require scalar synchronization on accelerators. Autograd follows the underlying QR/SVD requirements; rank deficiency, repeated singular values and subspace-selection boundaries can make derivatives undefined.

Examples

>>> tensor = torch.diag(torch.tensor([1., 1e-6, 1e-12], dtype=torch.float64))
>>> with tk.svd_method('qr_svd'):
...     u, s, vh = tk.utils.accurate_svd(
...         tensor, recursion_threshold=1e-4, max_depth=2)
>>> torch.allclose((u * s.unsqueeze(-2)) @ vh, tensor)
True
tensorkrowch.utils.truncated_svd(tensor, rank=None, cutoff=None, atol=None, rtol=None, cum_percentage=None, svd_method=None, return_info=False)[source]#

Computes a truncated SVD. If no truncation criterion is specified, it returns the full SVD. If more than one criterion is specified, the final rank is the minimum one, i.e. the one imposed by the most restrictive criterion.

Parameters

  • tensor (torch.Tensor) – Tensor to be decomposed, with shape (*, m, n) where * denotes zero or more batch dimensions.

  • rank (int, optional) – Maximum number of singular values to keep.

  • cutoff (float, optional) – Minimum singular value to keep. It must be finite and non-negative. Singular values <= cutoff are removed.

  • atol (float, optional) – Absolute tolerance over the tail sum of squared singular values. Starting from the smallest singular value, values are discarded while the accumulated sum of squares is <= atol. It must be finite and non-negative.

  • rtol (float, optional) – Relative tolerance over the tail sum of squared singular values. Starting from the smallest singular value, values are discarded while the tail sum of squares divided by the total sum of squares is <= rtol. It must be finite and in [0, 1].

  • cum_percentage (float, optional) –

    Minimum fraction of squared singular-value mass to keep. Equivalent to setting rtol = 1 - cum_percentage. It must be finite and in [0, 1].

    \[\frac{\sum_{i \in \{kept\}}{s_i^2}}{\sum_{i \in \{all\}}{s_i^2}} \ge cum\_percentage\]

  • svd_method ({"svd", "qr_svd"}, optional) –

    Exact backend used to compute the economy-size SVD. "svd" calls torch.linalg.svd() directly. "qr_svd" first reduces the larger matrix dimension with QR. If omitted, it uses the active value from get_svd_method(), whose initial default is "svd". The active backend can be changed globally with set_svd_method(), or temporarily with the svd_method() context manager. These configuration mechanisms also select the backend for higher-level methods that call truncated_svd() internally. Recursive tail refinement can independently be enabled with svd_method(..., refine=True) or set_svd_refinement(). It is disabled by default.

    Note

    Backward through "qr_svd" follows the differentiability requirements of torch.linalg.qr(): the input needs full column rank in the tall case and full row rank in the wide case.

  • return_info (bool) – If True, also returns _TruncatedSVDInfo with the full and selected ranks, the total and discarded squared norms, their per-batch values and the effective SVD backend. The complete singular value spectrum is not retained in this record.

Returns

By default, returns (u, s, vh) from an exact economy-size SVD after truncation. u has shape (*, m, r), s has shape (*, r), and vh has shape (*, r, n), where r is the selected final rank. If return_info=True, returns (u, s, vh, info).

Return type

tuple

Raises

  • TypeError – If tensor is not a torch.Tensor or svd_method is not a string, if rank is not an integer, if a tolerance is not a real number, or if return_info is not boolean.

  • ValueError – If rank is not positive, a tolerance is not finite or lies outside its accepted interval, or svd_method is not accepted.

  • RuntimeError – If tensor has fewer than two dimensions, as raised by torch.linalg.svd().

Examples

>>> tensor = torch.randn(4, 4)
>>> u, s, vh = tk.utils.truncated_svd(tensor, rank=2)
>>> len(s)
2
